content: Frozen shoulder, also known as adhesive capsulitis, is a condition characterized by pain and a progressive loss of motion in the shoulder joint due to inflammation. Symptoms of Frozen Shoulder: The primary symptoms include: A significant reduction in shoulder mobility. Persistent pain in the shoulder. Stiffness in the joint. In cases where the cause is unknown, the condition typically begins with pain, which limits arm movement. This lack of movement leads to increased stiffness and further restriction of motion. Over time, individuals may find it difficult to perform everyday activities, such as reaching overhead or behind their back. Causes of Frozen Shoulder: The shoulder joint is surrounded by a capsule made up of ligaments that stabilize the bones of the shoulder. When this capsule becomes inflamed, it restricts the free movement of the shoulder bones within the joint. Risk Factors: While frozen shoulder often occurs without a clear cause, certain factors increase the risk, including: Cervical disc disease in the neck. Diabetes. Previous shoulder injuries. Shoulder surgeries. Open-heart surgery. Hyperthyroidism. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will diagnose frozen shoulder based on the patient’s symptoms and a physical examination of the shoulder. A hallmark finding is the loss of rotational movement in the shoulder. X-rays may be performed to rule out other conditions, such as arthritis. In some cases, an MRI may reveal inflammation, but there are no definitive imaging signs specific to frozen shoulder. When to Seek Medical Attention: If you experience shoulder pain and stiffness and suspect frozen shoulder, it is important to consult a healthcare provider for appropriate evaluation and treatment. Treatment Options: Pain Management: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroid injections are commonly used to alleviate pain. Physical Therapy: Combining steroid injections with physical therapy can improve shoulder mobility. However, progress may take weeks, and full recovery can take 6 to 9 months. Physical therapy is intensive and requires daily commitment. Natural Resolution: If left untreated, frozen shoulder may resolve on its own within approximately two years, often with minimal long-term loss of motion. Addressing Risk Factors: Conditions such as diabetes or thyroid disorders should be managed to reduce the risk of recurrence. Surgical Intervention: Surgery is considered if non-surgical treatments fail. Under anesthesia, the healthcare provider may manipulate the shoulder to release scar tissue and restore motion. Arthroscopic surgery can also be performed to cut tight ligaments and remove scar tissue. Post-surgery, repeated pain blocks may be used to facilitate participation in physical therapy. Prognosis: With therapy and NSAIDs, most individuals regain shoulder motion and function within a year. Even without treatment, frozen shoulder often improves on its own within 24 months. However, surgery requires continued physical therapy for weeks or months to prevent recurrence. Treatment may fail if the patient cannot tolerate physical therapy. Potential Complications: Persistent stiffness and pain despite therapy. Rarely, a fracture of the arm may occur if the shoulder is forcefully manipulated during surgery. Prevention: The best way to prevent frozen shoulder is to seek medical attention promptly if shoulder pain limits your range of motion for an extended period. Early treatment can help avoid stiffness. For individuals with diabetes, maintaining good control of blood sugar levels can reduce the likelihood of developing frozen shoulder.
